title: Recruiting screen - Jordan Lee (Software Engineer, Inference)
summary: Initial recruiting screen for SWE (inference). Discussed Jordan's background in model serving, latency/cost tradeoffs, experience with Kubernetes and GPU optimizations, availability, and next steps for loop. Agreed to send take-home and schedule technical interview.
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-03-12
Start time: 16:30 PST
Duration: ~30 minutes
Attendees: Sophie Patel (Redwood), Carlos Mendez (Redwood), Aisha Khan (Redwood), Jordan Lee (Candidate)

[00:00] Sophie: Hey Jordan, great to meet you. I'm Sophie, I'm on the recruiting team at Redwood. Thanks for taking time today.
[00:12] Jordan: Hey Sophie, thanks for having me, yeah excited to chat.
[00:18] Sophie: Super quick intro, I'm gonna be coordinating the loop. Carlos is the hiring manager, Aisha will ask a couple technical questions. We'll run 25-ish minutes for this screen, and then we can talk logistics. Does that work?
[00:29] Jordan: Works for me.
[00:32] Carlos: Hi Jordan, I'm Carlos, I run the inference infra team. Quick icebreaker can you walk us through your recent role at VectorCloud and what you worked on related to model serving?
[00:45] Jordan: Sure. At VectorCloud I was on the serving team mostly building a unified inference platform for embeddings and text gen. I designed the autoscaler for GPU pools, worked on batching logic, prefix caching and a bunch of perf work. We used k8s with custom device plugins, and I did some kernel-level tuning for fp16 paths on A100s.
[01:09] Aisha: Nice. When you say prefix caching, is that like KV cache? how did you implement cache invalidation?
[01:17] Jordan: Yeah, it's basically KV cache we stored per-session keys in Redis with a small TTL and used a LRU policy plus version tags. We had a problem where long-running sessions could blow memory so we implemented windowing to drop stale prefixes.
[01:33] Carlos: Awesome. Did you also work on quantization or low-precision inference?
[01:38] Jordan: Some. I wrote a pipeline to convert checkpoints to 4-bit using bitsandbytes and tested out int8 paths too. We saw mixed quality tradeoffs; for retrieval-heavy embeddings we could go lower precision, for convo/text gen we kept fp16.
[01:55] Sophie: Quick logistics what's your current notice period and target comp band?
[02:00] Jordan: I'm on a 2-week notice. For comp I'm targeting around 180 to 210k base depending on equity and level.
[02:09] Sophie: Got it, thanks.
[02:12] Aisha: Tech question imagine a production endpoint that needs sub-100ms p95 latency for a 512-token gen, how would you approach that?
[02:21] Jordan: First I'd profile the whole stack measure token generation time, network hops, deserialization etc. Then I'd prioritize model selection and kernel optimizations: use quantized model if quality allows, tune batch sizes (maybe micro-batching), enable KV cache to avoid re-computation, and colocate the model on hardware with minimal NVLink hops. Also implement circuit breakers and fast-fail fallbacks to cheaper smaller models.
[02:47] Carlos: Do you have experience with routing by policy like splitting requests across dedicated and hosted capacity?
[02:53] Jordan: Conceptually yes we used rules based on latency SLOs and cost thresholds. Hot routes went to dedicated pools, colder traffic to spot instances. We had a fallback to a smaller model for overload.
[03:07] Sophie: Any familiarity with compliance VPC or KMS/HSM integrations? Customers often ask.
[03:12] Jordan: I've integrated KMS for key rotation and worked with our infra team on VPC peering for private deployments, yes.
[03:20] Aisha: Can you tell us about a tricky debugging incident you led?
[03:24] Jordan: One time we saw tail latency spikes traced it to a GC pause in a Python process doing batch assembly. Turned out memory fragmentation in a long-lived thread pool triggered intermittent GC. We rewrote the critical path in Rust, and moved batching into a native service which stabilized p99.
[03:42] Carlos: Nice. Do you have hands-on with CUDA or custom kernels?
[03:46] Jordan: Limited kernel dev, but I wrote bindings and optimized memory copies, and worked with vendor libs for fused attention. I'm comfortable reading kernel code and collaborating with low-level teams.
[03:58] Sophie: Cool. Loop logistics our interview loop is a coding + system design + team onsite. If things go well we'd do a take-home first (1 week), then schedule an interview with Aisha and others. Would you be open to a take-home?
[04:12] Jordan: Yep, that's fine.
[04:15] Sophie: Any constraints on scheduling the next round?
[04:18] Jordan: I'm flexible next week after 10am PT, except Thursday morning.
[04:24] Aisha: Small brainteaser how would you optimize batching for latency-sensitive short prompts vs cost-sensitive long prompts?
[04:32] Jordan: I'd do dynamic batching with latency bounds: maintain two scheduling classes, one for low-latency which disables batching beyond a tiny micro-batch, and a cost class that waits longer to accumulate larger batches. Use adaptive timers based on observed interarrival times. Also cache prefixes aggressively for short prompts.
[04:52] Carlos: Do you use any specific tooling for load testing and measuring per-token costs?
[04:56] Jordan: We used a combination of Locust for request-level load and a custom harness that replayed production traces to estimate token counts and cost. It wasn't perfect sometimes tokenization differences caused mismatches.
[05:10] Sophie: Anything else you'd like us to know about your background or interests?
[05:14] Jordan: I'm interested in infrastructure that bridges research to production, and I enjoy working on performance and reliability. Also open source contributor to a small inference library.
[05:26] Sophie: Great. We'll send the take-home, candidate instructions, and a calendar invite for the systems interview if you pass the take-home. We'll also share our benchmark doc if that's helpful.
[05:36] Jordan: That'd be helpful, thank you.
[05:39] Carlos: Ok recap sophie sends take-home and calendar options; Jordan completes take-home by 2025-03-15 if possible; Carlos to share benchmark doc and Aisha will prepare the system design prompt.
[05:52] Sophie: Any questions for us?
[05:54] Jordan: No, I think that's it. Thanks for the time.
[05:59] Sophie: Thanks Jordan, we'll be in touch.
[06:03] (call ends)

Notes: transcription includes occasional mis-heard words and abbreviations (k V cash / K-V cache, quantize Asian -> quantization).
